section.description: Twelve units that take you from your first Spanish word to a whole short conversation.

units.title: Your first words in Spanish
units.communicative_goal: Hear Spanish, read it aloud, and say your first five words.
units.objective: Hear Spanish, read it aloud, and say your first five words.

examples.note: the h is silent — say OH-la
ñ sounds like the ny in canyon
c before i sounds like s

question.prompt: The h in hola is silent. So how does hasta start?
question.explanation: The Spanish h is always silent — hola, hasta, hoy. You will never hear it, in any word.

question.prompt: Spanish also wishes you good luck. La suerte is feminine. Which one is it?
question.explanation: Describing words copy the noun's ending: masculine takes -o or -os, feminine takes -a or -as. That is the whole reason it is buenos días but buenas tardes.

dialogues.scenario: You pass a neighbour on the stairs in the morning.

question.prompt: You have met me llamo and te llamas. How would you say his name is Diego?
question.explanation: Spanish literally says I call myself. The little word does the work: me is myself, te is yourself, se is himself or herself — which is why you rarely need él or ella at all.

question.prompt: Diego is from Peru. Which one is right?
question.explanation: ser changes shape with who it is about: soy for I, eres for you, es for he or she. Add de plus a place and you have said where someone is from.

notices.title: Quiero, and then whatever you want

question.prompt: You want the bill. Which one?
question.explanation: Quiero means I want, and whatever you want goes straight after it — a thing (quiero un café) or an action (quiero comer). Nothing else has to change.

prompt.english: Good morning. What would you like to drink?

question.prompt: necesitar works exactly the same way. How do you say she needs help?
question.explanation: Change the ending, not the word order: hablo, hablas, habla — necesito, necesitas, necesita. Because the ending already says who, Spanish usually drops yo and tú entirely.

question.prompt: You want to ask how much it is. Which one?
question.explanation: qué, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, quién, por qué — every one of them opens the question, with the verb straight after. Spanish needs no extra word where English adds do.

question.prompt: You want to say there is a restaurant nearby. Which one?
question.explanation: hay says something exists, and takes un or una. está says where a particular thing is, and takes el or la. That is why it is hay un mercado but el banco está cerca.

notices.title: The weather is something Spanish makes

question.prompt: It is cool today. Which one?
question.explanation: Weather uses hacer: hace sol, hace frío, hace calor, hace fresco. How *you* feel is different — that uses estar: estoy cansado, estoy contento.

stories.title: Un día en Madrid
stories.setup: Ana writes a few lines about her day.

lines.english: Today I am in Madrid.
It is sunny, but it is cool.
I want to buy a coffee.

lines.spanish: El café está cerca de la casa.
lines.english: The café is near the house.
I am very happy.

questions.explanation: Hace sol, pero hace fresco — two weather expressions joined by pero, but.
Estoy muy contenta. She is talking about herself, so it is estar, not hacer.

dialogues.scenario: A friend messages you first thing in the morning.

prompt.english: Good morning. What's the weather like today?

notices.title: Spanish says it the other way round

examples.note: the same shape: Spain delights me

question.prompt: You have met me gusta and te interesa. How would you ask does she like coffee?
question.explanation: gustar, encantar and interesar all work backwards: the thing does the pleasing, and the little word says who it pleases. me = me, te = you, le = him or her. That is why it is me gusta and never yo gusto.

stories.title: Ana y Diego
stories.setup: Ana sits down at a café in Madrid and someone says hello.

lines.spanish: Ana está en un café en Madrid.
lines.english: Ana is at a café in Madrid.
Hello. My name is Ana. And you?
My name is Diego. Nice to meet you.
Where are you from?
I am from Mexico, but I live here.
What do you want to drink?
I want a coffee, please.
I like learning Spanish.

questions.explanation: Soy de México — de plus a place is where you are from.
…pero vivo aquí. pero — but — is what flips the sentence: from Mexico, living here.

questions.prompt: What does Diego want to drink?

dialogues.scenario: Someone sits down at your table.
The whole thing: meeting Diego, and ordering together.

prompt.english: Nice to meet you, Ana. Where are you from?
And what's the weather like today?

distractors: Hay un mercado en la calle.
